talks.summary:
### Overview
In this episode of FortiGuardLIVE, Derek Manky (VP of Global Threat Intelligence at Fortinet's FortiGuard Labs) and Aomar Marrakchi discuss the evolving landscape of ransomware settlements, criminal business models, and defensive strategies. Reflecting on over a decade of tracking ransomware since 2010, the speakers explore how attackers have transitioned from broad opportunism to highly organized, selective enterprise models targeting massive multi-million-dollar payouts.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Extortion and Wipers**: Ransomware playbooks have advanced beyond double and triple extortion into incorporating wipers. Previously confined primarily to Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) operations, wipers are increasingly leveraged by ransomware gangs to hinder post-incident forensic investigation by destroying evidence, as well as serving as intimidation to compel victims into paying.
- **Cryptocurrency Preferences**: Threat actors have largely shifted away from privacy-focused coins like Monero in favor of Bitcoin. While Monero offers built-in privacy, liquidating millions of dollars is difficult. Bitcoin provides broader liquidity, easier settlement access for victims paying seven-to-eight-figure ransoms, and simpler conversion and money laundering pipelines into real-world currency.
- **Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) Business Model**: The operational model has evolved from a pay-per-install (PPI) approach with thousands of unvetted actors to a pay-per-purchase (PPP) commission model. RaaS core operators now curate exclusive networks of vetted, skilled affiliates who receive the majority share of ransoms. These affiliates focus on high-value targets demanding seven- to eight-figure ransoms, leaving lower six-figure demands behind.
- **Diversified Distribution Vectors**: Ransomware deployment is increasingly distributed through an array of initial access vectors, including botnets, website and CMS plugins (such as WordPress plugins), ad networks, phishing campaigns, and macro-enabled office documents.

### Technical Details
Defending against contemporary ransomware requires mapping and disrupting complex attacker infrastructure rather than solely focusing on malware binaries. Infrastructure encompasses initial delivery mechanisms, vetted affiliate portals, command-and-control (C2) servers, money mule systems, and laundering networks. Proactive defenses highlight multi-layered prevention—incorporating endpoint security, web filtering, DNS filtering, and integrating threat intelligence into AI/ML-driven detection models to stop intrusions before encryption or data wiping begins.

### Takeaways
- **Incident Response as an Ongoing Practice**: Organizations should maintain active, tested incident response plans that adapt continuously to modern ransomware trends, including wiper recovery and antiforensic tactics, rather than treating incident response as a reactive measure activated only during a crisis.
- **Proactive 'Shift Left' Defense**: Given that ransomware settlements now reach tens of millions of dollars, the return on investment (ROI) heavily favors proactive defense and automation (AI-powered SecOps) to intercept threats early.

EMS endpoint profiles set malware protection, web filtering, application firewall rules and vulnerability scanning, and zero trust tags are built from checks such as Active Directory group membership, domain logon, antivirus status and BitLocker state. On the FortiGate, those tags feed ZTNA rules that match the source user, the published server or URL, and the required tags, with security inspection applied per resource. Access was tested for a remote engineer, an on-premises IT user, and an on-premises machine running an outdated Windows install with vulnerable applications, which was denied every resource. Client certificates issued by EMS verify each connection, and SAML lets a supported application log the user in without a second password prompt. The FortiGate logs record each allowed and denied attempt.

The second half covers FortiSASE, the cloud-delivered version that reuses the same tagging model for remote users and thin-edge sites. Web filtering blocks categories such as proxy avoidance and pornography for both. Enabling TLS inspection exposed malware hidden inside encrypted HTTPS sessions that had been invisible before. The practical takeaway is that access decisions can rely on device posture, not just identity, and that ZTNA and SASE can be combined.

talks.teaser: Shows how FortiGate SSL inspection decrypts traffic to block a malware download and a risky Facebook post.
talks.summary:
This short product demo argues that SSL inspection matters because most web traffic is now encrypted, and that a firewall which cannot read that traffic misses threats hidden inside it. It walks through the FortiGate SSL inspection security profile, which can decrypt outbound traffic to the internet and inbound traffic aimed at internal servers hosting applications, including several certificates for several applications. The profile sets how blocked and untrusted certificates are handled, whether server name mismatches are enforced, and whether protocol and cipher compliance applies. Administrators can exempt reputable sites, web categories, or address objects defined by FQDN, IP address, or geolocation from decryption.

The presenter then explains why deep inspection is also needed for application control, since many cloud file upload and download functions and most Facebook features can only be identified when traffic is decrypted. Decryption also helps prevent data exfiltration. The profile is attached to a security policy, and decrypted traffic can be mirrored to a server for archiving and analysis.

In the live demonstration, the profile first runs in certificate-based inspection mode. A malware download from an internal test server over HTTPS succeeds, and a Facebook wall post goes through even though the application control profile blocks it. After switching to custom deep inspection, the same malware download is decrypted, detected and blocked, and the Facebook post is blocked and logged. The antivirus logs show the blocked Grand Crab ransomware file, and filtering the application control logs by the Facebook post application shows the related entries. The takeaway for practitioners is that certificate-only inspection leaves encrypted threats and application policies unenforced.

talks.summary:
## Overview
This video demonstrates FortiGate's user identification feature in next-generation firewalls (NGFW) and covers both agentless and agent-based deployment configurations. The feature enables the firewall to map network traffic to specific users by consolidating user and group information from multiple sources, with all data available in the FortiGate dashboard's User tab.

## Information Sources
User information and IP mappings are pulled from:
- Active Directory
- RADIUS
- Syslog
- Exchange
- eDirectory
- Citrix Terminal Server

## Configuration Methods
Two primary approaches are detailed:

**Agentless Configuration (FSSO Polling)**: Fortinet Single Sign-On periodically polls Active Directory at fixed intervals to retrieve user information. Administrators define an LDAP server as the source and select specific Active Directory groups from which to pull user information.

**Agent-Based Configuration**: A collector agent is deployed on a server within the domain controller's network. The transcript mentions using 4D Authenticator as an example collector agent. This approach provides enhanced functionality, enabling the collection of user mapping information from additional sources including syslog servers, Citrix Terminal Servers, and Exchange servers.

## Implementation & Usage
Once the fabric connectors for identity are configured, administrators use the User Authentication tab to define user groups. These groups can be incorporated into security policies to control user access. All traffic traversing the FortiGate is mapped to specific users and can be viewed in the logs.

## Practical Demonstration
The video includes a live demo showing:
- A test user (Ron Smith) logged into a desktop behind the FortiGate
- User web traffic to allowed sites (YouTube, Yahoo) appearing in the Forward Traffic Logs with username mapping
- Blocked traffic (poker.com) recorded in web filtering logs with the associated username

All user activity is accessible through the Log and Report section, where the Forward Traffic Logs display all traffic with associated usernames, enabling granular visibility into who accessed what resources through the firewall.

## Key Benefits
User identification enables security policies and access controls based on user identity rather than IP addresses alone, and provides detailed audit trails linking specific network activity to individual users.

talks.teaser: Explores why ransomware keeps growing and whether cyber insurance and negotiated settlements can serve as a real defense.
talks.summary:
Derek Manke of Fortinet's FortiGuard Labs joins host Jim Richberg to describe the current ransomware landscape. He says activity jumped sharply in the first half of the previous year and has stayed high, and that payloads are becoming more targeted and destructive, with wiper features now combined with extortion. The pair link this growth to cryptocurrency, since criminals can move funds quickly across many coins and platforms. They also describe an ecosystem that has matured to the point of offering help desks that walk victims through buying crypto and making transfers.

The conversation then turns to cyber insurance, which organizations often see as a way to avoid dealing with criminals. Manke agrees it is a useful safeguard but argues it cannot be a silver bullet or a stopgap. Policies typically cover measurable costs such as fines and equipment replacement, but not business losses or reputational damage. Public sector bodies can be especially exposed, because their spending is published and attackers can estimate coverage limits. Paying a settlement also does not end the threat, since criminals often return for more and shift to other targets.

The speakers agree that ransomware needs a shared response involving governments, technology providers, insurers and organizations. Manke stresses that the basics come first, including strong security controls and offline backups, with insurance and negotiation considered only after other layers have been explored. The host notes that repeat victims may see insurers reduce payouts or withdraw coverage. The main takeaway is that insurance adds a layer of protection but does not replace prevention.

The senior engineer reviews the cloud-based automatic analysis, which flags an in-memory payload and a DLL named windbio.dll masquerading as a legitimate library. This short demo picks up from an earlier segment on manual remediation and shows how the FortiEDR platform can respond to threats automatically through playbooks. Playbooks set which actions run for each event classification, and different playbook policies can apply to different collector groups. The presenter reviews the notification options, which can send email, forward messages to a SIEM or open tickets in a system such as ServiceNow.

The investigation actions include isolating a device, either through the collector's own communication control or through a NAC integration such as FortiNAC. A playbook can also move an infected device into a stricter collector group with tighter policies until it has been analysed and cleaned. Out-of-the-box remediation covers process termination, file deletion, removal of malware persistence and blocking of threat communication at the firewall. Custom actions can be configured on the integration page and then appear in playbooks.

For the demo, the playbook is switched from simulation to protection. A malware sample is run on an endpoint and its file is deleted within seconds. Cloud analysis classifies the event as malicious, which triggers Active Directory actions that reset the user's password and log the user off, along with file deletion and blocking of the attacking IP address on FortiGate. A Metasploit run on a Linux device then produces a similar set of automatic responses in the event viewer. The main takeaway is that response actions can be tuned per classification and per group, and can be checked in simulation before enforcement is turned on.

## Overview
The FortiGate 3500F Series is a high-performance next-generation firewall (NGFW) from Fortinet designed to deliver industry-leading threat protection, intrusion prevention, and SSL inspection. The appliance is housed in a compact 2RU form factor while offering one of the highest port densities available on the market.

## Key Hardware and Design
The 3500F includes two high-availability 25 gigabit SFP28 slots, 30 standard 25 gigabit SFP28 slots, and six 100 gigabit QSFP28 slots. The 3501F variant adds two 2TB onboard SSDs for logging flexibility. Power redundancy is provided through two hot-swappable power supplies to optimize connection performance and reliability.

## Technical Architecture
The firewall leverages Fortinet's breakthrough security processing architecture. Three NP7 network processors work inline with FortiOS to deliver superior performance for multicast traffic, VPN, CGNAT, WAP, and IP tunnel acceleration. Eight CP9 content processors (Fortinet's 9th generation custom security processing units) handle pattern matching acceleration, application identification, pre-scan signature correlation, and real-time IPS signature matching to support the main CPU.

## Performance Specifications
The 3500F Series delivers exceptional throughput capacity: 595 gigabits per second firewall throughput, 165 gigabits per second IPsec VPN throughput, 72 gigabits per second IPS throughput, and 65 gigabits per second next-generation firewall throughput. Threat protection throughput reaches 63 gigabits per second. With the hyperscale license and NP7 processors, the device supports up to 5 million connections per second. The platform also provides elephant flow and VXLAN acceleration for hybrid and hyperscale data center deployments.

## Deployment Capabilities
The 3500F Series supports extensive deployment flexibility for network segmentation, secure web gateways, intrusion prevention systems, and mobile security. CGNAT is optimized for both 4G and 5G mobile security deployments. The appliance is positioned for deployment at the enterprise edge, in hybrid data center cores, or across internal network segments.

## Takeaways
The FortiGate 3500F Series is positioned as an ideal partner for large enterprises and service providers requiring high-performance, multi-layered security in a compact form factor. Its combination of specialized network and security processors, high port density, and substantial throughput capacity makes it suitable for complex network environments demanding both performance and comprehensive threat protection.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this FortinetLIVE session, Rick Peters, Field CISO for Operational Technology (OT) in North America at Fortinet, speaks with Troy Ament, Fortinet's Field CISO for Life Sciences and Healthcare. Together, they examine the intersection of critical infrastructure, operational technology, and healthcare security heading into 2022. The discussion highlights how the rapid digital transformation prompted by the COVID-19 pandemic expanded attack surfaces and attracted targeted adversary activity, creating critical challenges around operational resilience, supply chains, and clinical continuity.

### Key Topics
- **Digital Acceleration and Changing Attack Surfaces:** Over the course of the pandemic, healthcare organizations underwent massive shifts, including remote workforce mobilization (such as moving thousands of employees home in weeks), dramatic expansion of virtual visit platforms from roughly 100 to over 45,000 monthly visits in large systems, data sharing with local and state governments, and automated tracking of PPE and ICU capacities. In life sciences and pharmaceutical manufacturing, rapid vaccine production amplified visibility and made these organizations prime targets.
- **Evolution of Adversary Tactics:** While attackers largely held off targeting providers in the initial months of 2020, they soon exploited the strain on health systems. Spikes in ransomware caused major disruptions, prompting tens of millions of dollars in ransom demands. Attacks have also expanded beyond hospital facilities to upstream third-party cloud service providers offering payroll, staffing, billing, revenue cycle services, and electronic medical records (EMRs).
- **Convergence of Healthcare and Operational Technology:** Both OT and healthcare share critical dependencies on reliability and safety. Both sectors face high consequences from outages and must proactively protect distributed environments that span on-premises equipment, cloud platforms, and software-defined networking.

### Technical Details
- **Zero Trust and Multi-Factor Authentication:** Health systems are increasingly adopting Zero Trust principles to minimize blast radiuses and attack footprints. This adoption is accelerated by cyber insurance requirements, notably driving multi-factor authentication (MFA) adoption beyond previous ~70% levels.
- **Integrated Security Architecture:** The speakers advocate for moving away from fragmented tools toward integrated mesh or fabric-based security architectures that embed governance and protection directly into clinical workflows and business systems.
- **Behavioral Analysis and Telemetry:** Enhancing situational awareness requires utilizing behavioral analysis and data-driven visibility to recognize anomalous adversary activity early across IT, OT, and connected domains.

### Takeaways
- **Operational Downtime Awareness:** Executive leadership and CEOs now recognize that cyber incidents can cause two to three months of severe operational downtime, shutting down critical workflows such as EMR access and electronic prescription routing.
- **Maturing Security Operations:** Healthcare entities that weathered near-misses have demonstrated that investing in mature security operations centers and proactive defenses significantly reduces operational damage.
- **Collaborative Defense:** Cybersecurity in critical infrastructure cannot be tackled in isolation. Healthcare and OT organizations must treat cybersecurity as a team sport, working closely with external partners and peers to build resilience as threats evolve into 2022.

talks.title: Log4j Vulnerability | FortiGuardLIVE
talks.teaser: Examines how Log4j exploitation spread into many campaigns and why fast patching and layered detection matter.
talks.summary:
This FortiGuard Live interview opens with the host and Fortinet's field CTO framing the Log4j flaw as a long-running problem rather than a one-off event. They compare it with earlier incidents such as Conficker, Heartbleed and Shellshock, and note that the vulnerability has become a commodity, with at least ten separate campaigns reusing the exploit code within a few weeks.

The middle of the discussion covers how attacks are likely to change. Early exploitation relied on sending requests to web pages with a crafted host header, but the guest expects attackers to target any input that gets logged, including wireless and SMS-based systems. Fixes for the library moved through several versions in about a week, which the guest credits to a wider community review of small open-source projects that many products depend on, while also noting that attackers move just as fast. Software bills of materials are presented as a way for organisations to find where affected components sit in their networks. The malware seen so far includes ransomware, remote access trojans and crypto miners, many built as Linux ELF binaries aimed at servers and IoT devices.

The closing part makes the case for layered defence. Patching is essential, but the guests also point to IPS and web application firewall signatures, detection of new malware families, and scanners that look for the vulnerability itself. Because payloads are being obfuscated and changed, they recommend repeating checks rather than running a single scan. Fortinet's outbreak alerts are described as a way to look back at past activity and keep monitoring, while SOC services can help filter the very large volume of alerts. Listeners are pointed to Fortinet's threat research blog and threat signals for updates.

This sponsored podcast episode looks at the idea of a security fabric, an integrated set of products that share threat and posture information to help manage risk across the network and endpoints. Fortinet's director of systems engineering, Stephen Watkins, presents the concept as a platform approach rather than a collection of standalone devices.

The main contrast is with buying best-of-breed tools from several vendors. Watkins argues that multi-vendor setups rely on integration points that can break when one product is upgraded, leaving gaps in information sharing, policy enforcement and visibility, and that managing many consoles adds to the burden. He describes a fabric in which firewalls, intrusion prevention and other enforcement points exchange threat data in both directions, so policy can change dynamically when a specific threat is detected.

For zero trust, he explains that FortiOS runs as the firmware across FortiGate appliances, virtual machines and public cloud, combining next-generation firewalling, SD-WAN, routing and access proxy functions under one license. A single management plane extends to switches and wireless controllers, while FortiClient and EMS bring posture data from laptops and phones into the same policy model. The host questions whether tag-based approaches from other vendors work reliably across mixed device fleets. The takeaway is that simpler licensing and unified management, with consistent policy enforcement points, are what customers are asking for.

This sponsored podcast episode features Peter Newton, senior director of products and services at Fortinet, discussing zero trust network access (ZTNA). The host frames ZTNA as the successor to VPN-based remote access, driven by remote work and applications moving from on-premises data centres into public and private clouds. Newton's main point is that zero trust depends on continuous verification and per-application control, so user identity and device posture are rechecked for each session rather than only at the morning login.

Newton describes Fortinet's client-initiated model, where a FortiClient agent already on the endpoint reports posture details such as operating system version, antivirus presence and recent device events. He argues this is faster for users than a service-initiated model that requires a browser plugin download, and gives administrators more visibility into the device. Access is mapped through existing directory user groups and role-based rules enforced on the FortiGate, so organisations keep their current authentication systems. Single sign-on remains in use, and step-up multi-factor authentication can be triggered for unusual context or sensitive applications.

The discussion then covers licensing and performance. ZTNA is presented as an unlicensed feature on FortiGate devices running FortiOS 7.0.x firmware with FortiClient, and Newton links Fortinet's custom ASIC to keeping throughput high when several security functions are enabled. These are vendor claims. For practitioners, the practical takeaways are to check how ZTNA would plug into existing identity and device management, and to test the feature in a lab before deciding.

The administrator walkthrough covers five configuration steps on the FortiGate, with Azure AD setup treated as a prerequisite. The first step creates a CLI-based SAML identity provider and a user group, using the entity ID, sign-on and logout URLs from the Azure AD enterprise application, the imported Azure AD certificate, the user principal name claim as the username attribute, and the group's object ID. The next step creates an SSL VPN portal with tunnel mode, policy-based routing, a source IP pool and web mode enabled, plus a predefined bookmark. The third step enables SSL VPN settings on the chosen interface and port and maps the authentication to that portal.

The final step creates a firewall policy that runs from the SSL VPN tunnel interface to the internal network, uses the Azure AD-backed user group as the source, and allows the destination servers with all services turned on. For practitioners, the main takeaway is that the identifiers and URLs must match exactly between Azure AD and the FortiGate CLI, and the policy must reference the same group for the configuration to work end to end.

talks.summary:
Remote workers need VPN access, and organizations want one place to manage authentication and a second factor across their firewalls. This demo shows a FortiGate SSL VPN login that hands the first factor to Azure AD, with FortiAuthenticator acting as an identity provider proxy in front of it. FortiToken then supplies the second factor. The walkthrough covers both web mode and the FortiClient. In each case the login is redirected from FortiAuthenticator to Azure AD, and a push notification to the FortiToken mobile app completes the second factor. After connecting, the user reaches an internal web page, and the FortiGate shows the client's assigned address and services.

The presenter then checks the FortiAuthenticator and Azure AD logs, which record both the first and second factor for the session. The configuration is covered in order. In Azure AD, an application is created and set up for SAML single sign-on, with claims and the federation metadata exported and imported into FortiAuthenticator. Azure AD also needs a directory reader role for the application, and its client ID and client secret are entered into FortiAuthenticator. On FortiAuthenticator, a SAML service provider is created, its identity details are copied into the FortiGate CLI, and the FortiGate's entity and login URLs are returned to FortiAuthenticator. The FortiGate side then gets a user group mapping, an SSL VPN portal and settings, and a firewall policy for the tunnel interface. Finally, Azure AD users are imported into FortiAuthenticator, and a FortiToken Mobile token is activated by scanning a QR code from an emailed attachment.

The main takeaway is that a central identity proxy lets several FortiGates share one authentication and token management point. Attribute names and user groups must match across FortiGate, FortiAuthenticator and Azure AD, or logins will fail.

talks.title: Creating 3D Maps in FortiCentral | Fortinet
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a 3D site map in FortiCentral with walls, doors, windows, cameras and saved monitoring sectors.
talks.summary:
Gaps in camera coverage can leave a monitored site with blind spots exactly when footage matters most. This walkthrough shows how FortiCentral's 3D maps tool turns a floor plan into a three-dimensional model that displays camera locations, the angle of view in both directions, and the coverage range of each camera. The floor plan can be loaded from a file or captured from a web map, which provides the outside perimeter and a sense of scale.

The demo then builds the model in edit mode. Walls are traced over the floor plan by clicking points, with height and thickness adjusted by sliders, and misplaced points can be dragged, added or removed. Doors and windows are made by selecting a wall segment, enabling an opening on it, and setting the top and bottom edges. Walls can be recolored or given textures. Cameras are dropped in from predefined models or the device panel, then tuned for height, position, horizontal field of view and tilt, and a camera view mode shows what each one actually sees. A guard model is placed in the lobby as an example of a static element.

Finally, sectors are saved as named views of part of the map, such as a cafeteria or lobby, so each area can be monitored in its own pane. The takeaway for operators is that a carefully matched 3D model helps confirm coverage and reach the right camera feed quickly.

talks.title: Tech Bytes: Fortinet Secures Work-From-Anywhere With SD-WAN And ZTNA | Packet Pushers Podcast
talks.teaser: Explains how Fortinet combines SD-WAN and zero trust network access into one platform for remote and distributed workers.
talks.summary:
The podcast traces how SD-WAN has grown from branch link balancing into a platform that includes zero trust network access for distributed workers. The guests argue that remote users need checks on every application they reach, not a single check when they connect. Fortinet's approach combines the FortiGate access proxy, the FortiClient device agent and the EMS cloud policy and trust checks, so customers already running SD-WAN add only the agent and cloud policy.

The middle section covers the four ZTNA components and how existing VPN policies can be imported and extended with application-level business rules. The speakers contrast ZTNA with a traditional IPsec VPN, which typically authenticates once and then leaves the session broadly trusted. They also describe treating remote work locations as a separate segment that stays isolated from data center, corporate and internet segments, with the aim of raising the security floor across the whole network.

Near the end, the guests note that SD-WAN now accounts for a large share of Fortinet's revenue and that no separate license is needed for SD-WAN or the access proxy. For practitioners, the takeaway is to check whether an existing SD-WAN deployment can extend to zero trust access on one management platform rather than through another product.

talks.title: Tech Bytes: Protecting Public Schools With Fortinet’s Security Fabric | Packet Pushers Podcast
talks.teaser: Explains how a Nebraska school service unit runs shared Fortinet firewalls, log analysis and VPN for its districts.
talks.summary:
Bill Pulte, chief information officer of an educational service unit in Nebraska, describes how the unit provides shared services to public school districts, including internet access for its 18 districts. He explains that the state's Network Nebraska program steered many districts toward FortiGate firewalls, and that the unit chose Fortinet after an RFP because throughput held up as services such as antivirus, application control, intrusion prevention, web filtering and VPN were switched on.

The unit also runs FortiAnalyzer as a shared log collector. Its multi-tenancy lets each district see only its own logs, with about 1.5 terabytes allocated per district, and the device was sized for roughly 12 districts over a five-year term. Pulte argues that one shared appliance costs far less than separate purchases by each district. He notes that most districts only review logs after an incident, but that a state school insurer's cyber questionnaire may push them toward more proactive log analysis.

Pulte also recalls the pandemic, when staff moved to remote work within a day because the endpoint VPN client was already deployed and only group membership had to change, while student access proved harder. He closes by discussing plans to add endpoint security and Office 365 protections alongside the firewalls, and upcoming access point and phone system decisions that also lean toward Fortinet.

talks.title: Cloud and SD-WAN | FortinetLIVE
talks.teaser: Explains how multi-cloud SD-WAN and cloud on-ramp link branches to cloud workloads under consistent security policies.
talks.summary:
This interview segment features Vince from Fortinet talking with host Rob about multi-cloud SD-WAN and cloud on-ramp. The conversation opens with the pressures of heavy cloud use: most organizations now run hybrid or multi-cloud environments, and teams struggle to keep policies consistent while absorbing extra overhead for network, security and cloud operations.

Vince describes three things customers ask for: a simple way to connect from a branch or campus to the cloud, optimized performance for the workloads they reach there, and automation that makes the setup easier for users to manage. He argues that applications spread across clouds, regions and data centers should be interconnected so users stay unaware of where they run. He also warns that unmanaged clouds create visibility gaps that attackers can exploit, and recommends centralized control and visibility through a security fabric with consistent policies.

The pair then turn to Fortinet's announced integration with Google Cloud's Network Connectivity Center, which makes it easier to deploy FortiGate and SD-WAN into Google Cloud. Fortinet already supports Azure Virtual WAN and AWS, and offers middle-mile connectivity through Megaport. The main takeaway is that multi-cloud adds complexity that organizations have to accept, and the goal is to keep security, network and cloud operations simple and seamless on one platform.

talks.title: FortiGate Video Filtering Security | FortiOS 7.0
talks.teaser: Shows how FortiOS 7.0 video filtering blocks or allows YouTube videos by FortiGuard category and by channel ID.
talks.summary:
This short demo walks through the video filtering security service added in FortiOS 7.0. The service lets an administrator filter YouTube by FortiGuard categories, or by individual channel ID for finer control over one channel, user or video. The setup is a typical branch network in the Security Fabric, with a FortiAP connected to a FortiGate that acts as the wireless controller and a client attached to the access point. The video filter profile combines category filters with channel overrides, and the firewall policy is switched from flow mode to proxy mode, with the profile attached and SSL inspection set to deep inspection.

Before the filter applies, an unsigned YouTube session plays a music video without issue, and the FortiGate web filter logs show no video entry yet. The demo then covers three cases. A channel override blocks videos once the viewer signs in to the listed account, showing a replacement message and a blocked entry in the web filter logs with detail in the raw log view. A FortiGuard sports category block stops a sports video after a refresh, logged under that category. A knowledge category set to allow lets a video from a listed Fortinet channel keep playing.

The practical takeaway is that category rules and per-channel overrides can sit together in one profile, and that the logs confirm which action was applied to each video. The demo does not cover how the filter behaves on other platforms or with other SSL configurations.
